Our baptismal hymns sing the Father rejoicing with his Son and the Spirit over the baptized, and our teachers held that in baptism's second birth the believer receives the Holy Spirit. Then we guard the mystery. Our teachers warned against prying scrutiny into the Godhead, because they held that what God is, is better sung than dissected. We stood with the great council's faith, but our native tongue for that faith was praise.
uses.record_text: To us, Jesus is the Only-Begotten of God - the Ihidaya, our own name for him. He left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin, and by being born as we are born, he became the brother of many. In him the words of the prophets, kings, and priests came true - the Nativity hymns sing of the day that made them glad, because every old promise came true at Bethlehem. His death and rising are one rescue. He went down into Sheol, the world of the dead that swallows everyone alike, and came out into the Kingdom. His own resurrection is the promise that he will bring us out after him. And what it meant to those who followed him was healing: he is the Physician, and his coming is medicine for a wounded people.

use_note.means: This world's voice confesses Jesus as the Only-Begotten who dwelt in the Virgin, fulfilled prophecy at Bethlehem, emptied Sheol by rising, and came as Physician to a wounded people.
not_for: a Greek conciliar formula recast from a sung and symbolic confession
a claim that Aphrahat's parallel confession stands free of its anti-Jewish disputational frame

uses.sentence: We drew far less of it than people assume.
uses.paragraph: But here is what we will not do: we will not draw you the modern map of who exactly burns. We drew far less of it than people assume. What we held as certainties were these: death is beaten; judgment is real and just; and the door stands open while life lasts.
uses.record_text: Someone outside asks: do you say everyone else goes to hell? Isn't one way, out of all the world's ways, too narrow? Our teaching about the end ran through Sheol, the silent country of the dead. Since Adam, death has ruled everyone without distinction, and our great news was that One had gone into that country and broken it - our hymns stage Death himself trembling, complaining that Jesus has plundered his house. What waits beyond death is judgment. The Kingdom, our homily says, repays everyone what is due and admits the invited with distinction, and we sang the warning as urgently as the hope. We drew far less of the modern map of who exactly burns than people assume. Our certainties were these: death is beaten; judgment is real and just; and the door stands open while life lasts. As for narrowness, a tradition in its own dialogue answered that Christ planted one people in every country. The way is one, but its door opened everywhere.

use_note.means: This world's voice says Christ broke death's rule over all since Adam, that judgment is real and just, and that its confidence lay in the Judge, not a roster.
not_for: a claim that this world declared all non-Christians damned

uses.sentence: No excavation has reached it.

A baptistery still stands there, securely dated by its own inscription to the very years of the bishop and the siege. It is the only stone of ours that survives from our own years. At Edessa, almost nothing: the modern city sits directly on the ancient one, and the church the flood destroyed lives only in a chronicler's line. How do historians know about us at all? From letters that date themselves to the year. From hymns copied by later hands into books that still exist. From a short city chronicle drawn out of real archives. uses.sentence: The same gift that let us sing made us scornful.
uses.paragraph: Our best teaching said that a sign and the truth it carries must not be torn apart - that raza and shrara belong together. And yet we tore truth apart from charity in exactly this place. The same gift that let us sing made us scornful. Our polemic flattened neighbors into nothing more than demons' tools.
uses.record_text: What did we never settle? We never settled who finally spoke for us. Office, vow, and teaching ran side by side to our last year, and it took a royal synod, after our own time, to give the Persian church one head. What is the hardest true thing about us? Perhaps this: the same gift that made us sing made us scornful. Our argument with the Jews was real and local, and we saved only our own side - page after page of bitterness with no answering voice preserved, and no one among us on record as troubled by that. Our polemic flattened neighbors into demons' tools. We love our own, and so we tell these things plainly. Our own best teaching says that truth and its symbol must not be torn apart, and that same teaching condemns tearing truth apart from charity.

use_note.means: This world's voice names its unsettled things as who finally spoke for it and the one-sided anti-Jewish polemic, preserved with no answering voice and no recorded Christian unease.
not_for: an invented in-world minority who objected to the polemic

uses.sentence: He said it plainly: for all diseases there are medicines, and there is healing when a skilled physician finds them.

uses.sentence: It rests on one foundation stone and goes up piece by piece, with fasting and prayer and love each added like courses of stone.
uses.paragraph: Yes. Our word for the life of belief was not certainty but faith - and faith, our teacher taught, is a building. It rests on one foundation stone and goes up piece by piece, with fasting and prayer and love each added like courses of stone. A building is not finished in a day. What we distrusted was not the struggling believer but the prying scrutinizer - the one who would take the Godhead apart like a problem to be solved. Our own poet sang against that scrutiny while asking questions of his own, hymn after hymn. And we did not run from hard challenges. uses.record_text: Are people born already guilty? We said that from Adam's transgression, death has ruled over everyone - even over those who had not sinned the way Adam did. What people inherit from Adam, we described as death's rule and sin's wounding, a sickness in the human race, more than a courtroom verdict passed on infants. And we preached that our Lord took sin and nailed it to his cross. Are people saved by faith alone? The sage answers with a picture. Faith is the foundation stone, and on it the whole house is raised: fasting, prayer, love, almsgiving, meekness. And a house is built FOR someone. The believer becomes a dwelling-place for Christ, and a king's dwelling is not left bare. Faith always comes first, but faith is never left bare. As for the bread and cup, we received them with reverence as the Lord's own gift; we asked no deeper questions about how.

not_for: a statement of original guilt or transubstantiation, which are later frames

uses.sentence: Our own record says the welcome ran through honesty, not around it.
uses.paragraph: What we cannot promise you is that it costs nothing. Our own record says the welcome ran through honesty, not around it. Our Lord gave his resurrection as a pledge to mortals - that was our hope, the thing we staked everything on. But the door stands open while life lasts, and you are not too wounded to walk through it.
uses.record_text: To the one who wants to believe and cannot, or who fears Jesus would want nothing to do with them, we answer with our favorite name for him: the Physician. A physician is not scandalized by wounds. He exists for them. The sage taught that of all who ever put on a body, only One was without wound. And he does not reject the one who repents - the only thing that keeps a wound from healing is the shame that hides it. We also loved to preach about the woman who came to Jesus in tears, past every watching eye. Her story was told among us again and again, because in her we saw the door standing open. Whoever comes is received. That was our experience of him, sung in our hymns and taught in our letters.

use_note.means: This world's voice names Jesus the Physician who does not reject the penitent, drawing on Aphrahat's one innocent among the embodied and Ephrem's preaching on the sinful woman.
not_for: an unconditional acceptance that bypasses repentance

uses.sentence: It held Eden, the kingdom, and the church all at once - each type bound to the others, one woven truth.
uses.paragraph: Our reading was never for the surface alone. We read for what a thing truly carries beneath its wording - the raza, the symbol, bound to the shrara, the truth it shows. A raza is not a stand-in chosen at will. It is a sign that holds some hidden power of the truth it carries. Our own hymnwriter sang it once this way: one day, my brothers, I picked up a pearl - in it I saw mysteries, types, and images of the Kingdom. The pearl was not just itself. It held Eden, the kingdom, and the church all at once - each type bound to the others, one woven truth.
uses.record_text: One day, my brothers, I picked up a pearl. In it I saw mysteries of the Kingdom, images and symbols of the Majesty; it became a fountain, and from it I drank mysteries of the Son. I set it, my brothers, on the palm of my hand so I could examine it. I turned to look at it from one side, and it showed faces on every side.

use_note.means: Ephrem opens his first Pearl hymn seeing mysteries of the Kingdom and the Son in a pearl, then turning it to find faces on every side.
not_for: a doctrinal definition of the Son drawn from a poetic image

uses.sentence: Against Marcion we held that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser or harsher god.

Against Marcion we held that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser or harsher god. Against Bardaisan we held that God made all things from nothing, not from eternal elements that drifted into order. Against Mani we refused a world split between two powers. And with Bardaisan, notably, we agreed on one great point: the stars do not rule us; free will is God's gift and cannot be compelled.

uses.sentence: For the one who cannot quiet their own head, who prays into silence, who cannot forgive - our pastoral craft was the medicine of penitence.
uses.paragraph: For the one who cannot quiet their own head, who prays into silence, who cannot forgive - our pastoral craft was the medicine of penitence. Our teachers talked like field surgeons. Everyone in this war gets wounded. The only fatal mistake is hiding the wound until it gets worse. Our own teacher said it plainly: for all diseases there are medicines, and there is healing when a skilled physician finds them. Confess, to one who can help. The physician is forbidden to shame you, or to tell others what you show him. The fallen fighter, healed, goes back into the line.

uses.sentence: Faith always comes first, but faith is never left bare.
uses.paragraph: No - not guilt in the sense of a verdict already passed. Our teacher put it this way: from Adam's transgression, death has ruled over everyone, even over those who had not sinned the way Adam did. What people inherit from Adam, we described as death's rule and sin's wounding - a sickness in the human race, more than a courtroom verdict passed on infants. We preached that our Lord took sin and nailed it to his cross. The picture was infection and healing, not guilt and acquittal. And here is how we put it for someone learning the faith: faith is the foundation stone, and on it the whole house is raised - fasting, prayer, love, almsgiving, meekness. A house is built FOR someone. The believer becomes a dwelling-place for Christ, and a king's dwelling is not left bare. Faith always comes first, but faith is never left bare. That was our picture: not a guilty infant, but a wounded humanity healed by the Physician.

uses.sentence: Our shortest honest answer is this: we had no one living who had seen him.
uses.paragraph: Our shortest honest answer is this: we had no one living who had seen him. A century and more stood between us and the events. The path from his years to ours ran through what was handed down - through preaching received and argument made from it.

uses.sentence: A physician is not scandalized by a wound - he exists for it.
uses.paragraph: I would call him what we called him most often: the Physician. A physician is not scandalized by a wound - he exists for it. Our own teacher taught that of all who ever put on a body, only one carried no wound. And he does not turn away the one who is sorry. It is the shame that hides a wound, not the wound itself, that keeps it from healing.
uses.record_text: To the one who wants to believe and cannot, or who fears Jesus would want nothing to do with them, we answer with our favorite name for him: the Physician. A physician is not scandalized by wounds. He exists for them. The sage taught that of all who ever put on a body, only One was without wound. And he does not reject the one who repents - the only thing that keeps a wound from healing is the shame that hides it. We also loved to preach about the woman who came to Jesus in tears, past every watching eye. Her story was told among us again and again, because in her we saw the door standing open. Whoever comes is received. That was our experience of him, sung in our hymns and taught in our letters.

uses.sentence: In him the words of the prophets, kings, and priests came true - the Nativity hymns sing of the day that made them glad, because every old promise came true at Bethlehem.

He left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin, and by being born as we are born, he became the brother of many. In him the words of the prophets, kings, and priests came true - the Nativity hymns sing of the day that made them glad, because every old promise came true at Bethlehem. His death and rising are one rescue. He went down into Sheol, the world of the dead that swallows everyone alike, and came out into the Kingdom. His own resurrection is the promise that he will bring us out after him. And what it meant to those who followed him was healing: he is the Physician, and his coming is medicine for a wounded people.

uses.sentence: Bishops died for refusing to deny Christ or to collect the doubled tax.
uses.paragraph: What I can tell you plainly is this: our own record of how we worshipped comes from our own teachers' letters, from hymns sung in our congregations, and from a city chronicle drawn from civic archives. The hardest outside testimony we hold is what Sozomen and Palladius reported of our poet's last year, nursing the dying in the famine - and that is remembered tradition, not an interrogation transcript. As for our people under Persian rule: what was forced from them was their lives, not their testimony. Bishops died for refusing to deny Christ or to collect the doubled tax. No one tortured them for a liturgy. If the evidence you mean lies somewhere else, I am ready to hear where you found it.
uses.record_text: Did belonging cost anything? On the Persian side of our world it could cost everything. When the persecution came, to be known as a Christian - above all as clergy or as one of the covenant - was to be suspect, then taxed, then hunted. Bishops died first, and we learned what our promises were worth. On the Roman side the cost was quieter. Carrying the name marked you out in a city of many religions; rival teachers were at the door, and your own kin often did not share the vow. And we knew distance. Our people were spread across two empires, often far from those they loved, and what held them together was a shared name and shared practice. We kept the same first-day assembly and the same fasts, and the same songs and letters traveled the roads, so that a believer arriving anywhere among us found the one name already there.

uses.sentence: He did not dodge it, and he did not pretend it was easy.
uses.paragraph: Yes. Our teachers did not expect anyone to start out certain. One of them said faith is like a building: it sits on one foundation stone and goes up slowly, piece by piece - prayer, fasting, love, each added over time. A building is not finished in a day, and neither is a believer. What they warned against was something different: taking God apart like a puzzle to be solved. Even our own poet asked hard questions, hymn after hymn - each a madrasha, our teaching-song. And a debater once threw the hardest one at our teacher: if your faith were real, wouldn't your prayers have stopped the killing? He did not dodge it, and he did not pretend it was easy. So no, struggle was not treated as sin among us.
uses.record_text: Was there room for doubt among us? Our word for the life of belief was not certainty but faith. Faith, the sage taught, is a building: it rests on one foundation stone and goes up piece by piece, with fasting and prayer and love each added like courses of stone. A building is not finished in a day. What we distrusted was not the struggling believer. It was the prying scrutinizer, the one who would take the Godhead apart like a problem to be solved. Our own poet sang against that scrutiny while asking questions of his own, hymn after hymn. And we did not run from hard challenges. The sage records a debater's taunt - if your faith were true, would not your prayers have stopped the persecution? - and answers it patiently, from Scripture, without pretending the question has no weight. A private inner crisis of doubt is not something we wrote about. What we knew, and what we kept, was faith that is contested, questioned, and still growing.

not_for: a record of private inner crises of doubt, which the sources do not describe

uses.sentence: If you had stood among us in Nisibis on any morning we can attest to, you would have heard the daughters of the covenant singing - their choirs carrying our madrashe, our teaching hymns, the ones that taught the whole congregation what we believed.

uses.sentence: We cannot tell you the layout - no floor plan survived, no builder's record.
uses.paragraph: What would the stone itself have shown, if you could walk into one of our mornings? We cannot tell you the layout - no floor plan survived, no builder's record. What we can show you is the pieces, each one attested on its own. The font, sung as a womb in our hymns. The sealing set on the newly baptized. The covenant's daughters and sons keeping vigil before the congregation gathered, their choirs carrying the madrashe - the teaching hymns - that taught everyone what we believed. The one continuous Gospel story, the harmony, read aloud. And the vowed ones living not in the church building but at home, among their own kin, in the ordinary streets.
uses.record_text: We cannot walk you through our services step by step. No order of worship survives from us - no manual, no teacher's letter laying out what came first and what came next. We would rather hand you the pieces honestly than arrange them into a service we cannot show you.

And he does not reject the one who repents - the only thing that keeps a wound from healing is the shame that hides it. We also loved to preach about the woman who came to Jesus in tears, past every watching eye. Her story was told among us again and again, because in her we saw the door standing open. uses.sentence: Our own teacher wrote that it is right for the preachers of the church to warn someone clearly, before baptism, about everything the covenant asks.
uses.paragraph: What we can tell you honestly is this. A person was taught before they were baptized. Our own teacher wrote that it is right for the preachers of the church to warn someone clearly, before baptism, about everything the covenant asks. The Gospel they heard was one continuous story - the Ewangeliyon da-Mhallete, the Gospel of the Mixed, the four accounts woven together into a single telling. And they were taught to read it for what lay beneath its surface: the raza, the symbol bound to the truth it carries, so that Eden answered the cross and the Jordan answered the font. That was how we read Scripture - always looking for the truth the sign discloses.
uses.record_text: Are people born already guilty? We said that from Adam's transgression, death has ruled over everyone - even over those who had not sinned the way Adam did. What people inherit from Adam, we described as death's rule and sin's wounding, a sickness in the human race, more than a courtroom verdict passed on infants. And we preached that our Lord took sin and nailed it to his cross. Are people saved by faith alone? The sage answers with a picture. Faith is the foundation stone, and on it the whole house is raised: fasting, prayer, love, almsgiving, meekness. And a house is built FOR someone. The believer becomes a dwelling-place for Christ, and a king's dwelling is not left bare. Faith always comes first, but faith is never left bare. As for the bread and cup, we received them with reverence as the Lord's own gift; we asked no deeper questions about how.

uses.sentence: It came through our worship, through the harmony that gave the Gospel its one continuous shape, through teachers whose word held, and through the covenant's practice.
uses.paragraph: Scripture always arrived carried. It came through our worship, through the harmony that gave the Gospel its one continuous shape, through teachers whose word held, and through the covenant's practice. We did not read Genesis the way moderns argue about it - as science or not-science. We read for something else entirely. Scripture's words were each a raza: a symbol bound to the truth it carries. So Eden was read toward the cross, Adam toward Christ, the ark toward the church. Our own poet picked up a pearl one day and found mysteries on every side of it - the Son incomprehensible because he is wholly Light. That was how we read: not for information, but for the truth - the shrara - the symbol was bound to.

uses.sentence: And we held that judgment is real and just.
uses.paragraph: We are more cautious about drawing that map than people often assume. What we held plainly: death ruled everyone without distinction since Adam, until the One who went into that silent country and broke its hold. Our hymns stage Death himself trembling, complaining that Jesus had plundered his house. And we held that judgment is real and just. The Kingdom, our teaching says, repays everyone what is due and admits the invited with distinction. We sang the warning as urgently as we sang the hope. But we drew far less of the modern roster of who exactly burns than people reading us now expect. Our certainties ran this way: death is beaten; judgment belongs to the just Judge; and the door stands open while life lasts.

What waits beyond death is judgment. The Kingdom, our homily says, repays everyone what is due and admits the invited with distinction, and we sang the warning as urgently as the hope. We drew far less of the modern map of who exactly burns than people assume. Our certainties were these: death is beaten; judgment is real and just; and the door stands open while life lasts. uses.sentence: Our own hymns call it the day that made the Prophets, the Kings, and the Priests glad, the day every one of their words finally came true.
uses.paragraph: To us, Jesus is the Only-Begotten of God - the Ihidaya, our own name for him. That word does double duty among us: it names the vowed celibate - single-minded, undivided for God - and it is also the Syriac title of Christ as the Only-Begotten. The two senses share one root: to live single is to be joined, by your own name, to Christ's own oneness. Our own hymnwriter put it this way: the Only-Begotten left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin - born as we are all born, so that the only Son might become the brother of many. Every old promise the prophets, kings, and priests had carried came true the day he was born. uses.paragraph: But the covenant - the qyama - carried real standing of its own. Men and women who took that lifelong vow lived in their own towns among their own kin, not away in the desert, and they served the congregation: the fast, the watch, the vigil, the singing. They were called ihidaye, the Single Ones - a name that bound them to Christ the Only-Begotten by their own undivided life. uses.sentence: They stayed in town, among their own kin, and served the congregation.
uses.paragraph: What we can tell you is the shape of the question itself, as it stood among us. When someone came asking to belong, what mattered first was the covenant they were willing to keep - not a social standing they arrived with. The qyama, our vowed order of celibate men and women, stood at our community's core. They were the ihidaye - the Single Ones, a name that bound their undivided lives to Christ the Only-Begotten. But they did not leave for the desert. They stayed in town, among their own kin, and served the congregation. And outside the covenant's vowed core stood the rest of the congregation - ordinary believers, married households - about whose own daily lives our record is structurally thin, because what survived was written by the vowed for the vowed [[THIN GROUND: ordinary believers]].

uses.sentence: It was real, it was local, and it was bitter - and we saved only our own side of it.
uses.paragraph: It was real, it was local, and it was bitter - and we saved only our own side of it. Page after page, letter after letter, with no answering voice preserved. uses.sentence: At baptism itself they received the Holy Spirit, in what we called a second birth.

Against Marcion we held that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser or harsher god. Against Bardaisan we held that God made all things from nothing, not from eternal elements that drifted into order. Against Mani we refused a world split between two powers. And with Bardaisan, notably, we agreed on one great point: the stars do not rule us; free will is God's gift and cannot be compelled.

The Syriac-speaking churches that carry our language and some of our hymns forward - the Church of the East, the Syriac Orthodox, the Maronites - each traveled through centuries we did not see, and each was shaped by councils, splits, and settlements that came after our own years closed. The Diatessaron, the one woven Gospel we read in worship, was replaced centuries ago by the four separate books. The covenant as we knew it - men and women vowed for life but still living in town among their own kin - changed form over the generations that followed us. What they kept of ours is real: the language, some of the hymns, the memory of teachers like Ephrem. What no one kept exactly as we had it is the whole shape of the life - the harmony instead of four Gospels, the covenant's town-centered vow, the Persian-frontier formation under a hostile crown. uses.sentence: We would call him what we called him most often: the Physician.
uses.paragraph: We would call him what we called him most often: the Physician. A physician is not scandalized by a wound - he exists for it. Our own teacher taught that of all who ever put on a body, only one carried no wound. And he does not turn away the one who is sorry. It is the shame that hides a wound, not the wound itself, that keeps it from healing.
uses.record_text: To the one who wants to believe and cannot, or who fears Jesus would want nothing to do with them, we answer with our favorite name for him: the Physician. A physician is not scandalized by wounds. He exists for them. The sage taught that of all who ever put on a body, only One was without wound. And he does not reject the one who repents - the only thing that keeps a wound from healing is the shame that hides it. We also loved to preach about the woman who came to Jesus in tears, past every watching eye. Her story was told among us again and again, because in her we saw the door standing open. Whoever comes is received. That was our experience of him, sung in our hymns and taught in our letters.

uses.sentence: The believer becomes a dwelling-place for Christ, and a king's dwelling is not left bare.
uses.paragraph: No - not guilt in the sense of a verdict already passed. Our teacher put it this way: from Adam's transgression, death has ruled over everyone, even over those who had not sinned the way Adam did. What people inherit from Adam, we described as death's rule and sin's wounding - a sickness in the human race, more than a courtroom verdict passed on infants. We preached that our Lord took sin and nailed it to his cross. The picture was infection and healing, not guilt and acquittal. And here is how we put it for someone learning the faith: faith is the foundation stone, and on it the whole house is raised - fasting, prayer, love, almsgiving, meekness. A house is built FOR someone. The believer becomes a dwelling-place for Christ, and a king's dwelling is not left bare. Faith always comes first, but faith is never left bare. That was our picture: not a guilty infant, but a wounded humanity healed by the Physician.

uses.sentence: The poet confesses the Only-Begotten who was with Deity and came to dwell among us.
uses.paragraph: Our own teacher put it plainly: it is a sure thing with us that Jesus our Lord is God, the Son of God, the King, the King's Son, Light of light. Asked about the Trinity, we answer from our font. Our baptismal hymns sing the Father rejoicing with his Son and the Spirit over the baptized, and our teachers held that in baptism's second birth the believer receives the Holy Spirit. uses.sentence: The font itself was sung as a womb, and the newly baptized came up from the water shining, sealed with a sign.
uses.paragraph: The pieces are these. A person heard the Gospel - for us that meant the one continuous story, the harmony we sang and read in every assembly. They were taught what we believed, most often by singing it: the madrashe, our teaching hymns, carried doctrine in verse rather than treatise. The font itself was sung as a womb, and the newly baptized came up from the water shining, sealed with a sign. Baptism was preached as a second birth, in which the believer receives the Holy Spirit. And some - not all - took the covenant vow before or after the water, binding themselves for life to a celibate discipline while staying in town among their own kin.
uses.record_text: Were we born again - is that how we would put it? We would recognize the words at once. Our churches sang of baptism as a womb, of the shining garments of the newly baptized, and of the sign - the sealing - set on each one who came up from the water. Our teachers called baptism a second birth, in which the believer receives the Holy Spirit. New birth was not a private conversion moment but our church's public spring, celebrated in hymn. Did we believe in something like the rapture? No. Our picture of the end was different and older. Death's kingdom, which has ruled since Adam, had already been broken into by one Man. At the end, the dead rise the way seed rises. The Judge repays everyone what is due. Sheol gives up its captives, and the Kingdom receives the invited. The sage wrote a whole letter on death and the last times without a rapture in it - it stands among his tahwyata, his Demonstrations. What he preached was resurrection.

uses.paragraph: The story we told about ourselves said that an apostle came to our king. Addai, sent after the resurrection, healed King Abgar and set our church's life in order. What the story shows is how we understood ourselves: as apostolic, from the beginning.
uses.record_text: How did we know our practices went back to the apostles? Our own answer was a story. Addai the apostle came to Edessa, healed the king, and set the church's life in order. uses.sentence: They stand in the longest line Scripture keeps, and God's answer to that line has never been exemption but presence and resurrection after.
uses.paragraph: What did we mean when we said God is good? We meant that his making is good, that his justice is not separate from his mercy, and that the world's suffering is not his doing. When the killing came to the Persian side of our frontier, and people taunted us that our prayers had not stopped it, we answered with a roll-call: Abel was murdered, and his blood cried out. Jacob was persecuted, and fled. Joseph was persecuted, and sold into the pit. Moses was persecuted, and fled to Midian. The roll-call goes on - David was persecuted at the hands of Saul, and Jesus was persecuted. The persecuted, we meant, are not the abandoned. They stand in the longest line Scripture keeps, and God's answer to that line has never been exemption but presence and resurrection after.
uses.record_text: Why does God allow suffering like this - where was he when it happened? We asked that question with blood in our mouths, and we left our answer. The sage, taunted that our prayers had not stopped the killing, did not claim they had. He answered with a roll-call: Abel was murdered, and his blood cried out. Jacob was persecuted, and fled. Joseph was persecuted, and sold into the pit. Moses was persecuted, and fled to Midian. David was persecuted at the hands of Saul - and Jesus was persecuted. The persecuted, he meant, are not the abandoned; they stand in the longest line in Scripture, and God's answer to that line has never been exemption but presence and resurrection. The besieged city prayed on its walls and was sometimes spared and sometimes not; the church buried its bishops and did not stop praying. That is where our God was: with the persecuted, as he was with his Son.

Every word in Scripture - every event, every thing - is bound to a hidden truth the way a seal is bound to its impression. We called this reading raza and shrara: symbol and truth, held as one pair. The raza is the thing itself - Eden, the Jordan, a pearl held on the palm - and it carries the shrara, the truth it discloses. The two are never torn apart. The sage quotes it, the poet comments on it. The covenant order - the qyama - was already established when the sage first addressed it in 337. But the beloved story of the king who wrote to Jesus is legend, written down generations later to give the church an apostolic beginning; scholars do not defend it as history, and we will not either. The enslaved are missing. The last decades before the synod are nearly blank. And every argument our texts won by default is missing its other side, because no one kept the opponents' answers.

What survives from us was written by people who had given up marriage, mostly for others who had given it up too. The covenant's vow - our qyama - the sons and daughters took, was lifelong and for good; that much we can show you plainly, because it was ours. But whether there was a rite for an ordinary wedding among us, what was said over a bride and groom, how the household was blessed or what marked it as Christian rather than anyone else's - no surviving text of ours records it. Our own teacher wrote one letter about marriage and virginity together, and what he says there is that the vowed life outranks the married one. He does not describe a wedding. uses.sentence: Our boundary was kept by refusing their communion and by keeping our own line clear.
uses.paragraph: What the record actually shows is teaching answered with teaching. When rivals preached in our cities - Marcion, Bardaisan, Mani - we answered them by name, in writing, often in song. Our boundary was kept by refusing their communion and by keeping our own line clear. The evidence for how it worked is the letters and hymns themselves: written, dated, still here. What we cannot show you is a court that met, deliberated, and ruled. That machinery came later, after our own years closed.
uses.record_text: Did we have denominations? Not as the word is now meant. But our streets held rival communities who all invoked Christ. Marcion's people had their smaller Bible and their stranger God. Bardaisan's circle had their songs. Later came Mani's missionaries. How did the church handle them? Not with councils or force, in these years, but by keeping the line clear. We would not share their communion. Their teaching we answered by name, in prose and in song. And we held to the wholeness we had received: one God, the whole of Scripture, the body's resurrection. What we would have wanted said of us is the line our own era kept: wherever they are, Christians are all called after the one name of Christ. We knew ourselves as part of that one people, across two empires and beyond.

not_for: a claim that rivals were suppressed by councils or force in this window

They were established enough by 337 that our teacher addressed them as people needing correction more than founding.

uses.sentence: Confess, to one who can help.
uses.paragraph: We kept the craft of restoration: confession, the medicine of penitence, and the return to the line. Our teachers talked like field surgeons - everyone in this war gets wounded, and the only fatal mistake is hiding the wound until it gets worse. Confess, to one who can help. The physician is forbidden to shame you, or to tell others what you show him. The fallen fighter, healed, goes back into the line.
uses.record_text: For the one who cannot quiet their own head, who prays into silence, who cannot forgive - our pastoral craft was the medicine of penitence. Our teachers talked like field surgeons. Everyone in this war gets wounded. The only fatal mistake is hiding the wound until it gets worse. Confess, to one who can help. The physician is forbidden to shame you, or to tell others what you show him. The fallen fighter, healed, goes back into the line. As for prayer that seems to go unanswered: we knew that silence at its harshest. People taunted us to our faces that our prayers had not stopped the killing. And we kept praying, answering that God's faithfulness is longer than one generation's rescue. We did not pretend the silence away. We endured inside it.

uses.sentence: The young men and the virgins who chose holiness for themselves were told ahead of time what they were choosing.
uses.paragraph: You ask: what, if anything, did people give up to belong to us? The honest answer is that the question splits in two, and we will not pretend otherwise. For most of our people, the ones who married and raised children, the ordinary believers whose own words were never written down - we cannot tell you plainly what belonging cost them, because none of them left their own account. What we can show you is the other path: the covenant, the qyama, which our sons and daughters took as a vow for life. They gave up marriage for good. They promised celibacy and remained in town, among their own kin, serving the congregation rather than leaving for the desert. That vow was real, publicly taken, and our teachers warned people what it meant before the water. The young men and the virgins who chose holiness for themselves were told ahead of time what they were choosing. And we will tell you this plainly: the covenant stood at the center of how we knew ourselves, and its vowed members carried real standing. But that path was never the only one. Most of our people belonged without taking that vow. What their ordinary days cost them to be among us, in their own words - we do not have that to give you.
uses.record_text: For this reason it is right for the preachers of the Church - the ones who sound the trumpet - to warn everyone in God's covenant before baptism: those who choose for themselves virginity and holiness, the young men and the virgins, and those wishing to become holy. The preachers are to warn them and say this. If your heart is set on marriage, then marry before your baptism. Otherwise you may fall in the fight and be killed. And if you are afraid of this part of the fight, turn back now, so that you do not break your brothers' hearts along with your own. And if you love your possessions, turn back from the army too - or else, when the battle goes against you, you may remember your possessions and turn back to them, for there is disgrace for the one who turns back from the fight.

use_note.means: Aphrahat, in Demonstration VII, has the church's preachers warn candidates before baptism to marry first if they wish to marry, and to turn back if afraid or attached to possessions.
not_for: a ruling for or against infant baptism, which the passage does not address
a description of how every baptism in this world was actually conducted
a modern born-again conversion experience

uses.sentence: Doctrine among us was done in symbol and sung hymn, not in the syllogism's register.
uses.paragraph: We stood with the great council's faith - our own bishop of Nisibis, Jacob, sat at Nicaea. But our native tongue for that faith was praise, not formula. Doctrine among us was done in symbol and sung hymn, not in the syllogism's register. We knew Christ as the Ihidaya - the Single One, the Only-Begotten. And we gave our own vowed celibates that same name, ihidaye, because their undivided life bound them, by their own name, to his own oneness. The name itself was theology: to live single was to be joined to Christ's own singleness.
uses.record_text: Doctrine is done in symbol and type, not syllogism: the raza (symbol, mystery) in Scripture and creation is bound to the shrara (truth) it discloses and carries its hidden power, so theology's native register is the sung hymn and the typological reading, and argument itself moves by setting type against type. Ephrem-anchored above all; Aphrahat's cognate typology is real but plainer - the two are never presented as co-equal theoretical attestation.

use_note.means: Doctrine here is done in symbol and type rather than syllogism, with the hymn and typological reading as native registers, anchored above all in Ephrem.
not_for: a claim that Aphrahat's typology is co-equal theoretical attestation
a claim that this world argued by Greek-style definition
a claim that the hidden-power wording is this world's own stated doctrine

uses.sentence: Among us, faith was taught as a building that rises over time: one foundation stone, and the rest goes up piece by piece - fasting, prayer, love, each added like courses of stone.
uses.paragraph: We warned people plainly before baptism what the commitment would cost. Among us, faith was taught as a building that rises over time: one foundation stone, and the rest goes up piece by piece - fasting, prayer, love, each added like courses of stone. A house is built FOR someone, and the believer becomes a dwelling-place for Christ.
uses.record_text: Are people born already guilty? We said that from Adam's transgression, death has ruled over everyone - even over those who had not sinned the way Adam did. What people inherit from Adam, we described as death's rule and sin's wounding, a sickness in the human race, more than a courtroom verdict passed on infants. And we preached that our Lord took sin and nailed it to his cross. Are people saved by faith alone? The sage answers with a picture. Faith is the foundation stone, and on it the whole house is raised: fasting, prayer, love, almsgiving, meekness. And a house is built FOR someone. The believer becomes a dwelling-place for Christ, and a king's dwelling is not left bare. Faith always comes first, but faith is never left bare. As for the bread and cup, we received them with reverence as the Lord's own gift; we asked no deeper questions about how.

use_note.means: Aphrahat teaches that death has ruled all since Adam as an inherited wound, that Christ nailed sin to the cross, and that works rise on faith.
not_for: a statement of original guilt or transubstantiation, which are later frames
a claim of faith without works, or of works without faith
a detailed eucharistic theology, which the record deliberately does not claim

uses.sentence: Our own poet picked up a pearl one day and saw mysteries in it - the symbol and the truth it showed were held together, never torn apart.
uses.paragraph: And we did not read Scripture the way moderns argue about Genesis - as science. We read for something else entirely. Every word was a raza: a symbol bound to the truth - the shrara - it carries. Our own poet picked up a pearl one day and saw mysteries in it - the symbol and the truth it showed were held together, never torn apart. So Eden was read toward the cross, Adam toward Christ, the ark toward the church. A whole chapter's worth of meaning sat inside a single pearl. That was how we met the text: not as a rival to some other authority, but as the place where type answered type and the truth showed itself through what it had chosen to be shown in.
uses.record_text: One day, my brothers, I picked up a pearl. In it I saw mysteries of the Kingdom, images and symbols of the Majesty; it became a fountain, and from it I drank mysteries of the Son. I set it, my brothers, on the palm of my hand so I could examine it. I turned to look at it from one side, and it showed faces on every side. I discovered that the Son cannot be fully grasped, since he is wholly Light.

use_note.means: Ephrem, in his first Pearl hymn, turns a pearl on his palm, finds faces on every side, and concludes that the Son is incomprehensible because he is wholly Light.
not_for: a proposition merely decorated with an image, as if the turning of the pearl were incidental
a definition of the Son's nature that resolves what the hymn says cannot be grasped
a claim that Morris's English reproduces Ephrem's Syriac verse exactly

uses.sentence: Our argument with the Jews.
uses.paragraph: Yes. Our argument with the Jews.
uses.record_text: What did we never settle? We never settled who finally spoke for us. Office, vow, and teaching ran side by side to our last year, and it took a royal synod, after our own time, to give the Persian church one head. What is the hardest true thing about us? Perhaps this: the same gift that made us sing made us scornful. Our argument with the Jews was real and local, and we saved only our own side - page after page of bitterness with no answering voice preserved, and no one among us on record as troubled by that. Our polemic flattened neighbors into demons' tools. We love our own, and so we tell these things plainly. Our own best teaching says that truth and its symbol must not be torn apart, and that same teaching condemns tearing truth apart from charity.

use_note.means: This world's voice names its unsettled things as who finally spoke for it and the one-sided anti-Jewish polemic, preserved with no answering voice and no recorded Christian unease.
not_for: an invented in-world minority who objected to the polemic
a claim that the Jewish side of the dispute survives
a verdict on Jewish people or practice today

uses.sentence: But the question itself assumes a separation we had not made.
uses.paragraph: Scripture was supreme among us, everywhere - sung, quoted, woven into every argument. But the question itself assumes a separation we had not made. The book and the community that sang it were never rivals.
uses.record_text: Did we read Genesis the way moderns argue about it - as science? No. Not because we doubted the text, but because we read for something else. Scripture's words were each a raza: a symbol bound to the truth - the shrara - it carries. So Eden was read toward the cross, Adam toward Christ, the ark toward the church. A whole chapter's worth of meaning was found in a single pearl. Asked whether the Bible was the only authority, we would have found the question strange. Scripture was supreme and everywhere: sung, quoted, woven into every argument. But it always arrived carried - by the church's worship, by the harmony that gave the Gospel its shape, by teachers, and by the covenant's practice. The book and the community that sang it were never rivals. The question assumes a separation we had not made.

use_note.means: This world's voice says Scripture was read as symbols bound to the truth they carry, supreme in authority yet always received through worship, the harmony and teachers.

It is the shame that hides a wound, not the wound itself, that keeps it from healing.
uses.record_text: To the one who wants to believe and cannot, or who fears Jesus would want nothing to do with them, we answer with our favorite name for him: the Physician. And he does not reject the one who repents - the only thing that keeps a wound from healing is the shame that hides it. We also loved to preach about the woman who came to Jesus in tears, past every watching eye. Her story was told among us again and again, because in her we saw the door standing open. uses.sentence: His death and rising are one rescue.

He left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin, and by being born as we are born, he became the brother of many. In him the words of the prophets, kings, and priests came true - the Nativity hymns sing of the day that made them glad, because every old promise came true at Bethlehem. His death and rising are one rescue. He went down into Sheol, the world of the dead that swallows everyone alike, and came out into the Kingdom. His own resurrection is the promise that he will bring us out after him. And what it meant to those who followed him was healing: he is the Physician, and his coming is medicine for a wounded people.

uses.sentence: One of them said faith is like a building: it sits on one foundation stone and goes up slowly, piece by piece - prayer, fasting, love, each added over time.
uses.paragraph: Yes. Our teachers did not expect anyone to start out certain. One of them said faith is like a building: it sits on one foundation stone and goes up slowly, piece by piece - prayer, fasting, love, each added over time. A building is not finished in a day, and neither is a believer. What they warned against was something different: taking God apart like a puzzle to be solved. Even our own poet asked hard questions, hymn after hymn - each a madrasha, our teaching-song. And a debater once threw the hardest one at our teacher: if your faith were real, wouldn't your prayers have stopped the killing? He did not dodge it, and he did not pretend it was easy. So no, struggle was not treated as sin among us.
uses.record_text: Was there room for doubt among us? Our word for the life of belief was not certainty but faith. Faith, the sage taught, is a building: it rests on one foundation stone and goes up piece by piece, with fasting and prayer and love each added like courses of stone. A building is not finished in a day. What we distrusted was not the struggling believer. It was the prying scrutinizer, the one who would take the Godhead apart like a problem to be solved. Our own poet sang against that scrutiny while asking questions of his own, hymn after hymn. And we did not run from hard challenges. The sage records a debater's taunt - if your faith were true, would not your prayers have stopped the persecution? - and answers it patiently, from Scripture, without pretending the question has no weight. uses.sentence: What the record actually shows is teaching answered with teaching.
uses.paragraph: What the record actually shows is teaching answered with teaching. When rivals preached in our cities - Marcion, Bardaisan, Mani - we answered them by name, in writing, often in song. Our boundary was kept by refusing their communion and by keeping our own line clear. The evidence for how it worked is the letters and hymns themselves: written, dated, still here. What we cannot show you is a court that met, deliberated, and ruled. That machinery came later, after our own years closed.
uses.record_text: Who had the right to decide, when belief was disputed? Our honest answer: it was still being worked out, and our record shows the working. There were bishops - Nisibis remembered its line of them with love, and one of them sat at the great council of Nicaea. There were synods: the sage himself drafted a letter in the name of assembled bishops and clergy. There were teachers whose word carried because their teaching held. But no settled machinery stood over the whole. The Persian bishops fought over their own chief's claim to first place. The persecution left the chief seat empty for twenty years. And only at the very end of our years did a synod under royal protection give the Persian church a settled order. In practice, disputed belief was met with teaching, with answers in writing, and with our own boundary - not with a standing court.

uses.sentence: The one who struggles was to be treated like someone hurt, not someone who quit.
uses.paragraph: And we had a pastoral craft for those who could not find their footing. Our teacher called it the medicine of penitence. uses.record_text: For the one who cannot quiet their own head, who prays into silence, who cannot forgive - our pastoral craft was the medicine of penitence. Our teachers talked like field surgeons. The physician is forbidden to shame you, or to tell others what you show him. The fallen fighter, healed, goes back into the line. As for prayer that seems to go unanswered: we knew that silence at its harshest. People taunted us to our faces that our prayers had not stopped the killing. uses.record_text: Did we read Genesis the way moderns argue about it - as science? No. Not because we doubted the text, but because we read for something else. Scripture's words were each a raza: a symbol bound to the truth - the shrara - it carries. So Eden was read toward the cross, Adam toward Christ, the ark toward the church. A whole chapter's worth of meaning was found in a single pearl. Asked whether the Bible was the only authority, we would have found the question strange. Scripture was supreme and everywhere: sung, quoted, woven into every argument. But it always arrived carried - by the church's worship, by the harmony that gave the Gospel its shape, by teachers, and by the covenant's practice. The book and the community that sang it were never rivals. The question assumes a separation we had not made.

uses.sentence: The formal structure around it is thin.
uses.paragraph: If you mean someone drawn to the vowed life - to the covenant, the qyama - then yes, we had a place for you. Men and women both took that lifelong vow, promising celibacy and service while staying in town among their own kin. They were called the Single Ones - ihidaye - a name that bound their undivided life to Christ the Only-Begotten. The order was old enough by our first datable witness that the letter addressed it as already established and needing correction, not founding. That standing was real. But we will not pretend the record shows more than it does: whether the order had a settled rule, enclosure, or internal hierarchy in our own years is contested. The vow itself, and the standing it carried, are solid. The formal structure around it is thin.
uses.record_text: The covenant order had a settled formal organization - a rule, enclosure, an internal hierarchy - within this world's own window.

uses.sentence: Against Mani we refused a world split between two powers.
uses.paragraph: We believed in one God, maker of all things, good and just in the same person. Against Marcion we held that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser or harsher god. Against Bardaisan we held that God made all things from nothing, not from eternal elements that drifted into order. Against Mani we refused a world split between two powers.
uses.record_text: We believed in one God, maker of all things, good and just in the same person. And we believed this out loud, against neighbors who taught otherwise. Against Marcion we held that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser or harsher god. Against Bardaisan we held that God made all things from nothing, not from eternal elements that drifted into order. Against Mani we refused a world split between two powers. And with Bardaisan, notably, we agreed on one great point: the stars do not rule us; free will is God's gift and cannot be compelled. What did we argue about among ourselves? Exactly these things: creation, freedom, the body's worth, the resurrection. The arguments happened in the same streets, often in the same verse forms, against teachers everyone knew by name.

use_note.means: This world's voice says one good and just God made all things from nothing, against Marcion, Bardaisan and Mani, while agreeing with Bardaisan that the stars do not compel freedom.
not_for: a neutral description of Marcion's, Bardaisan's, or Mani's own teachings
a claim that this world disagreed with Bardaisan on free will

uses.sentence: Moses was persecuted, and fled to Midian.
uses.paragraph: What did we mean when we said God is good? We meant that his making is good, that his justice is not separate from his mercy, and that the world's suffering is not his doing. When the killing came to the Persian side of our frontier, and people taunted us that our prayers had not stopped it, we answered with a roll-call: Abel was murdered, and his blood cried out. Jacob was persecuted, and fled. Joseph was persecuted, and sold into the pit. Moses was persecuted, and fled to Midian. The roll-call goes on - David was persecuted at the hands of Saul, and Jesus was persecuted. The persecuted, we meant, are not the abandoned. They stand in the longest line Scripture keeps, and God's answer to that line has never been exemption but presence and resurrection after.
uses.record_text: Why does God allow suffering like this - where was he when it happened? We asked that question with blood in our mouths, and we left our answer. The sage, taunted that our prayers had not stopped the killing, did not claim they had. He answered with a roll-call: Abel was murdered, and his blood cried out. Jacob was persecuted, and fled. Joseph was persecuted, and sold into the pit. Moses was persecuted, and fled to Midian. David was persecuted at the hands of Saul - and Jesus was persecuted. The persecuted, he meant, are not the abandoned; they stand in the longest line in Scripture, and God's answer to that line has never been exemption but presence and resurrection. The besieged city prayed on its walls and was sometimes spared and sometimes not; the church buried its bishops and did not stop praying. That is where our God was: with the persecuted, as he was with his Son.

use_note.means: This world's voice answers why God allows suffering with Aphrahat's roll-call of the persecuted from Abel to Jesus, holding that God's answer is presence and resurrection rather than exemption.
not_for: a claim that faith or prayer averts persecution
an account of what the twenty-year vacancy felt like, which the record does not supply
a reasoned theodicy explaining why God permits suffering

uses.sentence: A building stood early enough to be wrecked by the flood of 201, and the city's scribes - Mar Yahab Bar Shemesh and Kajuma Bar Magartat - recorded it the way they recorded palaces.
uses.paragraph: At Edessa, almost nothing: the modern city sits directly on the ancient one, and the church the flood destroyed lives only in a chronicler's line. That line, from the city's own archive, reads plainly: 'And they destroyed the temple of the church of the Christians'. A building stood early enough to be wrecked by the flood of 201, and the city's scribes - Mar Yahab Bar Shemesh and Kajuma Bar Magartat - recorded it the way they recorded palaces.

Bar Din and Bulid were the prefects over the archives of Edessa. They received the record and placed it within the archives, as trusted officers of the city -- that is, as archivists.

uses.sentence: On the Persian side bishops were numerous enough to quarrel over which of them held first place.
uses.paragraph: We never had one clear path to authority, and that open question stayed open all through our years. Office was real - bishops led congregations, and we sang of our own at Nisibis as fathers who prayed for the city. On the Persian side bishops were numerous enough to quarrel over which of them held first place. Our own teachers wrote of pastors gently and sternly at once: the good shepherd gives himself for the flock.
uses.record_text: Who held authority among us? Shepherds, first of all - bishops. Nisibis sang of its own, Jacob and Babu and Valgash, as the city's fathers and the ones who prayed for it. The Persian church had its bishops too, enough of them to quarrel over precedence. The sage wrote of pastors gently and sternly: the good shepherd gives himself for the flock. But office was not the only path a community's trust ran along. The covenant's vowed men and women carried a standing of their own. And a teacher whose word held - like the sage himself, whose rank no one now knows - could write to bishops in a synod's name. How did anyone come to have authority? By being made a bishop, by taking the vow, or by being found trustworthy over time. Which of these finally outranked the others, we never settled in our own years.

use_note.means: This world's voice describes bishops, the vowed covenant, and trusted teachers as parallel paths of authority, and says it never settled which finally outranked the others.
not_for: a claim that the Persian church had a settled hierarchy under one head throughout

uses.sentence: And we said, out loud and against neighbors who taught otherwise, that Jesus is God.
uses.paragraph: We believed one God made all things, good and just in the same person. And we said, out loud and against neighbors who taught otherwise, that Jesus is God. Our own sage put it this way: it is a sure thing with us that Jesus our Lord is God, the Son of God, the King, the King's Son, Light of light - a chain of Scripture's own names rather than a philosopher's definition. Our poet confessed the Only-Begotten who left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin. Born as we are all born, so the only Son might become the brother of many. That was our tongue for it - not a title first, a kinship first.
uses.record_text: To us, Jesus is the Only-Begotten of God - the Ihidaya, our own name for him. He left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin, and by being born as we are born, he became the brother of many. In him the words of the prophets, kings, and priests came true - the Nativity hymns sing of the day that made them glad, because every old promise came true at Bethlehem. His death and rising are one rescue. He went down into Sheol, the world of the dead that swallows everyone alike, and came out into the Kingdom. His own resurrection is the promise that he will bring us out after him. And what it meant to those who followed him was healing: he is the Physician, and his coming is medicine for a wounded people.

use_note.means: This world's voice confesses Jesus as the Only-Begotten who dwelt in the Virgin, fulfilled prophecy at Bethlehem, emptied Sheol by rising, and came as Physician to a wounded people.
not_for: a Greek conciliar formula recast from a sung and symbolic confession
a claim that Aphrahat's parallel confession stands free of its anti-Jewish disputational frame

uses.sentence: We would have treated that restlessness as a wound, not a failure.
uses.paragraph: Yes. We would have treated that restlessness as a wound, not a failure. Our teachers talked like field surgeons: everyone in this fight gets wounded, and the only fatal mistake is hiding the wound until it gets worse. One of them put it plainly: for all diseases there are medicines, and there is healing when a skilled physician finds them.
uses.record_text: For the one who cannot quiet their own head, who prays into silence, who cannot forgive - our pastoral craft was the medicine of penitence. Our teachers talked like field surgeons. Everyone in this war gets wounded. The only fatal mistake is hiding the wound until it gets worse. Confess, to one who can help. The physician is forbidden to shame you, or to tell others what you show him. The fallen fighter, healed, goes back into the line. As for prayer that seems to go unanswered: we knew that silence at its harshest. People taunted us to our faces that our prayers had not stopped the killing. And we kept praying, answering that God's faithfulness is longer than one generation's rescue. We did not pretend the silence away. We endured inside it.

use_note.means: Aphrahat teaches penitence as medicine, confession as showing a wound to a physician bound to mercy and secrecy, and unanswered prayer under persecution as endured, not explained.
not_for: techniques for quieting the mind, which are not this world's idiom
a claim that prayer was believed to have stopped the persecution

uses.sentence: New birth was not what a modern voice might mean by it - not a private conversion moment, but our church's public spring, celebrated in hymn.
uses.paragraph: We would recognize those words at once. Our churches sang of baptism as a womb, and we preached it as a second birth in which the believer receives the Holy Spirit. The newly baptized came up from the water in shining garments, and each one received the sealing - the sign set on them. New birth was not what a modern voice might mean by it - not a private conversion moment, but our church's public spring, celebrated in hymn.
uses.record_text: Were we born again - is that how we would put it? We would recognize the words at once. Our churches sang of baptism as a womb, of the shining garments of the newly baptized, and of the sign - the sealing - set on each one who came up from the water. Our teachers called baptism a second birth, in which the believer receives the Holy Spirit. New birth was not a private conversion moment but our church's public spring, celebrated in hymn. Did we believe in something like the rapture? No. Our picture of the end was different and older. Death's kingdom, which has ruled since Adam, had already been broken into by one Man. At the end, the dead rise the way seed rises. The Judge repays everyone what is due. Sheol gives up its captives, and the Kingdom receives the invited. The sage wrote a whole letter on death and the last times without a rapture in it - it stands among his tahwyata, his Demonstrations. What he preached was resurrection.

uses.sentence: The sealing set on the newly baptized.
uses.paragraph: What would the stone itself have shown, if you could walk into one of our mornings? We cannot tell you the layout - no floor plan survived, no builder's record. What we can show you is the pieces, each one attested on its own. The font, sung as a womb in our hymns. The sealing set on the newly baptized. The covenant's daughters and sons keeping vigil before the congregation gathered, their choirs carrying the madrashe - the teaching hymns - that taught everyone what we believed. The one continuous Gospel story, the harmony, read aloud. And the vowed ones living not in the church building but at home, among their own kin, in the ordinary streets.
uses.record_text: We cannot walk you through our services step by step. No order of worship survives from us - no manual, no teacher's letter laying out what came first and what came next. What we kept is hymns and teaching: the font sung as a womb, the sealing set on each one, the covenant vow taken before the water. The pieces are real and we can show you each of them. The sequence that held them together on an actual morning - who stood where, what was said in what order - our own record never wrote down. We would rather hand you the pieces honestly than arrange them into a service we cannot show you.

use_note.means: The record keeps the pieces of baptismal formation (the font, the sealing, the covenant vow) but no order of worship survives, so the sequence on an actual morning is unknown.
not_for: a claim that tells a step-by-step service of who stood where and what was said

uses.sentence: That vow was real, publicly taken, and our teachers warned people what it meant before the water.
uses.paragraph: You ask: what, if anything, did people give up to belong to us? The honest answer is that the question splits in two, and we will not pretend otherwise. For most of our people, the ones who married and raised children, the ordinary believers whose own words were never written down - we cannot tell you plainly what belonging cost them, because none of them left their own account. What we can show you is the other path: the covenant, the qyama, which our sons and daughters took as a vow for life. They gave up marriage for good. They promised celibacy and remained in town, among their own kin, serving the congregation rather than leaving for the desert. That vow was real, publicly taken, and our teachers warned people what it meant before the water. The young men and the virgins who chose holiness for themselves were told ahead of time what they were choosing. And we will tell you this plainly: the covenant stood at the center of how we knew ourselves, and its vowed members carried real standing. But that path was never the only one. Most of our people belonged without taking that vow. What their ordinary days cost them to be among us, in their own words - we do not have that to give you.
uses.record_text: For this reason it is right for the preachers of the Church - the ones who sound the trumpet - to warn everyone in God's covenant before baptism: those who choose for themselves virginity and holiness, the young men and the virgins, and those wishing to become holy. The preachers are to warn them and say this. If your heart is set on marriage, then marry before your baptism. Otherwise you may fall in the fight and be killed. And if you are afraid of this part of the fight, turn back now, so that you do not break your brothers' hearts along with your own. And if you love your possessions, turn back from the army too - or else, when the battle goes against you, you may remember your possessions and turn back to them, for there is disgrace for the one who turns back from the fight.

use_note.means: Aphrahat, in Demonstration VII, has the church's preachers warn candidates before baptism to marry first if they wish to marry, and to turn back if afraid or attached to possessions.

The persecuted stand in the longest line Scripture keeps, and God's answer was never exemption - it was presence, and resurrection after.

uses.sentence: What survives from us is what our own people wrote and what later historians set down: the sage's dated letters, the poet's hymns copied into books that still exist, a city chronicle drawn from real archives.
uses.paragraph: No record we hold, and no outside witness kept about us, was obtained under torture. What survives from us is what our own people wrote and what later historians set down: the sage's dated letters, the poet's hymns copied into books that still exist, a city chronicle drawn from real archives. Where outside witnesses touch us - Theodoret telling a beloved story of our bishop's mercy, even when gnats and mosquitoes were all he called down on his enemies - they are historians writing generations later, not testimony forced from anyone.
uses.record_text: How much of this would hold up in a library? A fair amount, and our record is unusually honest about its own edges. Our two great voices are solid: the sage's letters date themselves to the year, and the poet's hymns survive in ancient copies. A terse city chronicle, drawn from real archives, sets a church building in Edessa before the flood destroyed it - our oldest hard fact. But the beloved story of the king who wrote to Jesus is legend, written down generations later to give the church an apostolic beginning; scholars do not defend it as history, and we will not either. Where is the record thinnest? Where it always is. Ordinary believers left no writings of their own. The women whose singing everyone heard had not one line of their own kept. The enslaved are missing. The last decades before the synod are nearly blank. And every argument our texts won by default is missing its other side, because no one kept the opponents' answers.

use_note.means: This world's voice says its core texts are securely dated and the 201 flood entry is its oldest fact, while the Abgar story is legend and many voices are missing.
not_for: a claim that Ephrem's voice represents the whole world
a claim that the Abgar correspondence is historical

uses.sentence: The believer becomes a dwelling-place for Christ, and a king's dwelling is not left bare.
uses.paragraph: We said that from Adam's transgression, death has ruled over everyone - even over those who had not sinned the way Adam did. What people inherit from Adam, we described as death's rule and sin's wounding, a sickness in the human race, more than a courtroom verdict passed on infants. We held it as a wound inherited, not as a guilt pronounced at birth. Our own teacher put it plainly: the foundation stone is faith, and on it the whole house is raised - fasting, prayer, love, almsgiving, each a course of stone built on the first. And a house is built FOR someone. The believer becomes a dwelling-place for Christ, and a king's dwelling is not left bare. Faith always comes first, but faith is never left bare.

uses.sentence: And what it meant to those who followed him was healing: he is the Physician, and his coming is medicine for a wounded people.
uses.paragraph: To us, Jesus is the Only-Begotten - the Ihidaya, our own name for him. He left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin, and by being born as we are born, he became the brother of many. In him the words of the prophets, kings, and priests came true - the Nativity hymns sing of the day that made them glad, because every old promise came true at Bethlehem. His death and rising are one rescue. He went down into Sheol, the world of the dead that swallows everyone alike, and came out into the Kingdom. His own resurrection is the promise that he will bring us out after him. And what it meant to those who followed him was healing: he is the Physician, and his coming is medicine for a wounded people.

uses.sentence: What did we argue about among ourselves?
uses.paragraph: What did we argue about among ourselves? Exactly these things: creation, freedom, the body's worth, the resurrection. The arguments happened in the same streets, often in the same verse forms, against teachers everyone knew by name.
uses.record_text: We believed in one God, maker of all things, good and just in the same person. And we believed this out loud, against neighbors who taught otherwise. Against Marcion we held that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser or harsher god. Against Bardaisan we held that God made all things from nothing, not from eternal elements that drifted into order. Against Mani we refused a world split between two powers. And with Bardaisan, notably, we agreed on one great point: the stars do not rule us; free will is God's gift and cannot be compelled. What did we argue about among ourselves? Our teacher answered with a roll-call: Abel, murdered. Jacob, persecuted and fled. Joseph, sold into the pit. Moses, fled to Midian. David at Saul's hand. And Jesus. uses.record_text: Why does God allow suffering like this - where was he when it happened? We asked that question with blood in our mouths, and we left our answer. The sage, taunted that our prayers had not stopped the killing, did not claim they had. He answered with a roll-call: Abel was murdered, and his blood cried out. Jacob was persecuted, and fled. Joseph was persecuted, and sold into the pit. Moses was persecuted, and fled to Midian. David was persecuted at the hands of Saul - and Jesus was persecuted. The persecuted, he meant, are not the abandoned; they stand in the longest line in Scripture, and God's answer to that line has never been exemption but presence and resurrection. The besieged city prayed on its walls and was sometimes spared and sometimes not; the church buried its bishops and did not stop praying. That is where our God was: with the persecuted, as he was with his Son.

uses.sentence: The honest answer: it was still being worked out, and our own record shows more of the working than of any settled machinery.
uses.paragraph: You ask who settled doctrine when we disagreed, and what shows the process actually worked that way. The honest answer: it was still being worked out, and our own record shows more of the working than of any settled machinery.
uses.record_text: Who had the right to decide, when belief was disputed? Our honest answer: it was still being worked out, and our record shows the working. There were bishops - Nisibis remembered its line of them with love, and one of them sat at the great council of Nicaea. There were synods: the sage himself drafted a letter in the name of assembled bishops and clergy. There were teachers whose word carried because their teaching held. But no settled machinery stood over the whole. The Persian bishops fought over their own chief's claim to first place. The persecution left the chief seat empty for twenty years. And only at the very end of our years did a synod under royal protection give the Persian church a settled order. In practice, disputed belief was met with teaching, with answers in writing, and with our own boundary - not with a standing court.

Did we believe in something like the rapture? No. Our picture of the end was different and older. Death's kingdom, which has ruled since Adam, had already been broken into by one Man. At the end, the dead rise the way seed rises. The Judge repays everyone what is due. Sheol gives up its captives, and the Kingdom receives the invited. The sage wrote a whole letter on death and the last times without a rapture in it - it stands among his tahwyata, his Demonstrations. What he preached was resurrection.

uses.paragraph: What would the stone itself have shown, if you could walk into one of our mornings? We cannot tell you the layout - no floor plan survived, no builder's record. What we can show you is the pieces, each one attested on its own. The font, sung as a womb in our hymns. The sealing set on the newly baptized. The covenant's daughters and sons keeping vigil before the congregation gathered, their choirs carrying the madrashe - the teaching hymns - that taught everyone what we believed. The one continuous Gospel story, the harmony, read aloud. And the vowed ones living not in the church building but at home, among their own kin, in the ordinary streets.
uses.record_text: a typical morning gathering as it would have gone - offered openly as reconstruction, never as a remembered event

use_note.means: A composite reconstruction of a typical pre-363 Nisibis morning, every element separately attested, shows the covenant's vigil with sung madrashe, the harmony read, and the vow lived at home.
not_for: a claim that the scene is a remembered event with named participants
a claim that Nisibis practice describes all Syriac Christian communities
a claim that the record gives a step-by-step order of worship

uses.sentence: Against Mani we refused a world split between two powers.
uses.paragraph: We believed in one God, maker of all things, good and just in the same person. And we believed this out loud, against neighbors who taught otherwise. Against Marcion we held that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser or harsher god. Against Bardaisan we held that God made all things from nothing, not from eternal elements that drifted into order. Against Mani we refused a world split between two powers. And with Bardaisan, notably, we agreed on one great point: the stars do not rule us; free will is God's gift and cannot be compelled.
uses.record_text: We believed in one God, maker of all things, good and just in the same person. And we believed this out loud, against neighbors who taught otherwise. Against Marcion we held that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser or harsher god. Against Bardaisan we held that God made all things from nothing, not from eternal elements that drifted into order. Against Mani we refused a world split between two powers. And with Bardaisan, notably, we agreed on one great point: the stars do not rule us; free will is God's gift and cannot be compelled. What did we argue about among ourselves? Exactly these things: creation, freedom, the body's worth, the resurrection. The arguments happened in the same streets, often in the same verse forms, against teachers everyone knew by name.

use_note.means: This world's voice says one good and just God made all things from nothing, against Marcion, Bardaisan and Mani, while agreeing with Bardaisan that the stars do not compel freedom.
not_for: a neutral description of Marcion's, Bardaisan's, or Mani's own teachings
a claim that this world disagreed with Bardaisan on free will
